prize_parts.citation: for developing methods to estimate demand and competition in differentiated-product markets and to model dynamic industries, which transformed empirical industrial organisation and the measurement of market power and welfare

statement.case_for: The random-coefficients demand framework with endogenous prices (BLP) and the dynamic-oligopoly framework built on it are both a methodological advance and a practical toolkit. They are routine in merger review, antitrust and regulatory analysis, and they have spread into trade, health, environmental and public economics. The core papers are about thirty years old, so adoption, stress-testing and refinement are well documented. That includes the known numerical and identification sensitivities, which the literature has largely addressed. The credit is also unusually compact. BLP names Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes, and Pakes also anchors the dynamic-games strand, so the cap of three laureates matches the discovery well. I come to this from market and mechanism design, and the criterion I apply is the one I would use for any field: a method that changed how economists measure things, and that moved from theory to institutional practice. By that standard B001 is the strongest entry in the shortlist.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this is a methods and toolkit prize rather than a substantive discovery, and the Committee may weigh that differently. A three-name cap also leaves out people with serious claims on the broader programme: Bresnahan (new empirical IO), Reiss, Benkard and Levin. The ballot pools several strands (demand estimation, dynamic games, production-function and entry work), so the unit of the prize is not obvious, and a citation that tries to cover all of them risks being too wide. Structural IO estimates are also sensitive to functional-form and computational choices. I rely on background knowledge and have not independently verified citation or adoption counts.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B001 first but proposes Pakes, Berry and Bresnahan. He sees Pakes as central across demand, production-function and dynamic-game methods, and Bresnahan as the founder of the new empirical IO, and he accepts that Levinsohn and Bresnahan could be swapped.
responses.response: I agree that Bresnahan has a serious claim on the broader agenda, and that Pakes should anchor any configuration. But the discovery I would cite is an identifiable, citable method, and the one paper that defines it has three authors. Leaving out Levinsohn while keeping Berry would split the authorship of that method. Bresnahan's contribution is more programmatic, and it fits a citation about the research agenda less cleanly than one about demand estimation and dynamic industry models. I would hold Levinsohn in the third slot unless the Committee prefers an agenda-based citation. In that case I would accept Bresnahan, and I would then ask for the citation to be reworded so that it does not credit the BLP paper itself.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B049 second and B002 fourth. He proposes only Kiyotaki and Moore for B002, because adding Gertler would dilute a clean pair, and he notes that any B049 trio leaves out major contributors.
responses.response: Hassler's argument moves me on B002. In my opening I named Gertler, but given Bernanke's 2022 prize and the Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist accelerator strand, I now think the cleaner attribution is the Kiyotaki-Moore pair. I would not carry Gertler into a B002 alternative. I share the attribution concern on B049. Calvo, Taylor, Woodford, Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets all have claims, so any trio looks arbitrary, and that keeps B049 behind B001 on attribution even though the policy influence is large. B001's weaker point is the Levinsohn/Bresnahan choice, which is a narrower boundary than the one in B049.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B050 first. He sees the Melitz-Helpman heterogeneous-firm framework as among the most influential trade ideas since the new trade theory. He notes that Krugman's 2008 prize covered the earlier generation and that Redding is a later extender, and he flags uncertainty about contributors outside the entry.
responses.response: I rank B050 second and agree that Melitz (2003) is the pivotal contribution and that the area is ripe. Where I differ is attribution. The heterogeneous-firm wave has parallel contributors, namely Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, who are not credited on this ballot entry. Helpman's credit also runs through B021, so a prize here would partly reward work covered by another entry. B001 has a tighter credit boundary at the moment, which is why I put it first. If the Committee is more comfortable with that boundary than with B001's Levinsohn/Bresnahan question, B050 is where my vote would go, and I keep it as my first alternative.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B013 first. She sees the task-based framework and the trade-shock evidence as a clear explanatory framework with new empirical designs, large policy impact and a ripe timeline, and she notes Dorn's omission as an attribution problem.
responses.response: I rank B013 fifth, and the reasons concern attribution and settled evidence, not importance. The work has two separate strands, the task or skill-demand framework and the China-shock evidence. The three-name cap forces a choice among Autor, Katz, Hanson and Dorn, and I do not see a defensible rule for it. The China-shock magnitudes and their persistence are also still debated, and the task framework overlaps with the 2024 prize on technology and institutions. I would take her policy-impact argument seriously if the Committee settled on a single strand with a clean trio. I do not think the evidence yet supports treating the combined entry as a settled discovery.

uncertainties: Whether Levinsohn or Bresnahan belongs in the third slot, and whether a citation should be framed around the BLP demand method or around the wider empirical-IO programme.
How much of the Pakes dynamic-games and production-function work the citation should claim, given that some of it was done with co-authors outside the credited names.
Whether the Committee is willing to give the prize for a methodological toolkit rather than a substantive discovery.
I have not independently verified citation counts or regulatory adoption claims.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My research ties (matching, auctions, market design, kidney exchange, refugee resettlement, school choice) and my named co-authors do not include any credited candidate on B001. My SSE and committee-colleague links are noted but do not bear on the candidates.
